title: A comet’s tail doesn’t trail behind it: it points away from the Sun
body: A comet’s tail isn’t a wake. As a comet nears the Sun, sunlight and the solar wind push its escaping gas and dust outward, so the tail streams away from the Sun whichever way the comet is travelling. On the way out of the inner Solar System the comet therefore flies **tail first**. There are usually two tails: a straight, narrow ion tail of glowing charged gas that follows the Sun’s magnetic field lines, and a dust tail of grains pushed by sunlight itself, which lag into a gentle curve. A tail can stretch beyond one astronomical unit, the distance from Earth to the Sun.

slides.alt: A comet’s orbit around the Sun with the comet drawn at four points. At every point its tail points directly away from the Sun, so on the outbound leg the tail leads the comet.
slides.caption: Arriving, the tail trails; leaving, it leads. It always points away from the Sun.

slides.heading: Why the tail points away from the Sun

left.label: Ion tail
left.text: Charged gas captured by the solar wind. Narrow and straight, pointing directly away from the Sun along magnetic field lines.

right.label: Dust tail
right.text: Grains pushed by the pressure of sunlight. Heavier, so they lag behind into a gentle arc.

slides.label: Earth’s diameter: how wide a comet’s coma, the cloud around its nucleus, can get
slides.text: The solid nucleus underneath is generally less than 60 km across. Both tails grow out of that cloud.

slides.question: What pushes a comet’s straight ion tail?
slides.explanation: Charged gas is swept along by the solar wind and follows the Sun’s magnetic field lines, pointing directly away from the Sun. The dust tail is pushed by sunlight and curves.

slides.heading: Ion tail or dust tail?

items.text: Pushed by the pressure of sunlight
Follows the Sun’s magnetic field lines

slides.explanation: Charged gas is swept straight out along the Sun’s magnetic field; heavier dust grains, pushed only by sunlight, lag behind into a curve.
